newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Hefty rice stocks seen checking Philippine prices.
newsitem.headline: Hefty rice stocks seen checking Philippine prices.

text.p: Ample Philippine rice stocks at the start of the year will help keep inflation in single digits in the first six months of 1997, officials and analysts said on Thursday.
The state-owned National Food Authority (NFA) said Philippine rice stocks rose by 26 percent to 1.739 million tonnes as of January 3 this year against 1.374 million tonnes a year ago.
"The country's total rice inventory as of January 3 is good for 79 days based on the average requirement of 22,000 tonnes per day," NFA director for public affairs Vicente Racho told Reuters.

Analysts said the inventories and prospects of a better harvest would help keep inflation within the government's target of between six and seven percent this year. Inflation was 8.1 percent in 1995 and 8.4 percent last year.
Inflation should remain in check despite a projected rice shortfall of up to 500,000 tonnes in the traditionally lean July-September period, they said.

"The projected rice shortfall in the third quarter would be easily met by cheaper rice imports. As long as the government anticipates the problem, prices should remain stable," said a senior Agriculture Department official who requested anonymity.
Rice, the staple food of the Philippines' 68 million people, carries a weighting of between 10 to 15 percent in the consumer price index, analysts say.

"Prospects of more rice supplies should temper any rise in inflation. I'm looking at an average rate of five to six percent this year partly because of better rice supplies," said Noel Reyes, vice president at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.

Philippine Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero has said unmilled rice output in calendar 1997 would reach 12 million tonnes against estimated production of 11.52 million tonnes in 1996 and 10.5 million tonnes in 1995.
Other agriculture officials have estimated the country's rice output in 1996 at a more conservative 11.3 million to 11.4 million tonnes.

Despite the higher supplies, demand will continue to grow, officials said. Escudero said he expected imports of between 300,000 and 500,000 tonnes of rice will be necessary this year to keep up with demand.

A rice shortage due to a bad harvest spiked inflation to 11.3 percent in September 1995. The consumer price index did not reach single-digit figures again until June 1996 after the government imported 800,000 tonnes of rice to meet the shortfall.

To head off a recurrence, President Fidel Ramos has ordered the NFA, traders and farmers to maintain combined rice stocks of 1.98 million tonnes beginning on July 1 to see the country through the July-September lean period.
Officials said the high stocks at the beginning of the year could help meet that goal.
"As long as NFA carries rice equivalent to the country's 25-day requirements in its warehouses starting July 1, then prices would be all right," the Agriculture department official said.
